body:
D'var Torah on Parshas Ki Sisa: The Strength of Being Human

Introduction: A Nation That Just Saw Sinai

Parshas Ki Sisa contains one of the most shocking moments in the Torah: the sin of the Golden Calf. Only weeks earlier, the Jewish people had stood at Har Sinai and heard the voice of Hashem. They had witnessed the miracles of the Exodus, the splitting of the sea, and the revelation that defined the birth of our nation. And yet, only a short time later, the Torah describes one of the greatest spiritual failures in our history.

The natural reaction when reading this story is disbelief. How could the same nation that saw so much fall so quickly into such a mistake? But the Torah is rarely telling stories simply to record history. Instead, it is revealing something about human nature and about the nature of our relationship with Hashem. In many ways, the story of the Eigel HaZahav forces us to confront a fundamental truth about Jewish life: in order to be a Jew, one must first be a human being.

We Are Not Malachim

Judaism never asks us to become angels. Malachim exist in an entirely different reality. They do not struggle with uncertainty, fear, or conflicting emotions. Human beings do. The Torah itself acknowledges this distinction in the well-known teaching that when Moshe Rabbeinu ascended to receive the Torah, the angels protested. They argued that the Torah should remain in heaven among spiritual beings rather than being given to people living in a physical world.

Moshe’s response was simple and profound. The Torah speaks about honoring parents, about business dealings, about jealousy, about mistakes, and about repentance. Angels do not live in that world. Human beings do. The Torah was therefore given to be lived in the complicated and sometimes messy reality of human life. The purpose of Torah is not to escape the world, but to elevate it.

Two Days That Reflect Our Humanity

Judaism regularly reminds us that we are human beings who serve Hashem through the physical world. Sometimes we rise above the physical for a short period of time, such as on Yom Kippur. On that day we wear white, refrain from physical pleasures, and attempt to reach a state that resembles the existence of the malachim. But the Torah also provides another model of holiness that looks completely different.

Purim celebrates joy, food, friendship, and physical celebration. Instead of separating ourselves from the world, we elevate the physical world itself. The Zohar even connects these two days directly.

פורים אתקריאת על שם יום הכפורים (תקוני זוהר נ״ז ע״ב)

Purim, the Zohar teaches, is called by the name of Yom HaKippurim. The comparison suggests that holiness can emerge through very different expressions. Sometimes it appears through restraint and separation from the physical. At other times it appears through elevating the physical itself. Both approaches acknowledge the same reality: Judaism is meant to be lived by human beings.

The Moment Everything Went Wrong

With this perspective, the story of the Golden Calf becomes easier to understand. Moshe Rabbeinu ascended Har Sinai and told the Jewish people that he would return after forty days. The commentaries explain that the people miscalculated the timing. Some counted from the wrong starting point, while others misunderstood whether Moshe would return during the fortieth day or after forty complete days had passed. Regardless of the precise calculation, the people believed Moshe had delayed.

The Torah describes the moment of crisis clearly.

וירא העם כי בשש משה לרדת מן ההר (שמות ל״ב:א)

The people saw that Moshe was late descending from the mountain. Without Moshe’s leadership, confusion spread quickly throughout the camp. Fear began to replace faith, and uncertainty led to a demand for something visible that could guide them forward. In that moment of weakness, the people turned to Aharon and demanded a physical symbol to lead them. That request ultimately resulted in the creation of the Eigel HaZahav.

A Stiff-Necked People

In describing the Jewish people, Hashem uses a striking phrase:

עם קשה עורף הוא (שמות ל״ב:ט)

A stiff-necked people.

At first glance this description sounds entirely negative. Stubbornness often leads to conflict and error. Yet the Torah frequently teaches that the same human qualities that lead to failure can also become sources of strength. Stubbornness can become rebellion, but it can also become persistence. It can become resilience. It can become the refusal to abandon faith even in the most difficult moments of history.

In fact, the very trait that led the Jewish people into this mistake would later become the trait that allows them to survive exile after exile. The Jewish people are stubborn, and sometimes that stubbornness creates problems. But it is also the same stubbornness that preserves the covenant with Hashem throughout centuries of challenge and hardship.
